svg.text: The world is asking for a way to slow AI agents down. A speed limit on a road with no lanes is not a control. These are the lanes — and who holds each one.
slower is not safer; a stopped agent is not
accountable, and a stale verdict still authorizes
What the calls to “slow down” are actually asking for
AI Kill Switch Act (July 2026) — the capability to slow or stop a system, on order
incident reporting; evidence a third party can examine after the fact
< 50% of CISOs can say what their agents can access or are authorized to do
a revoked helper stops NOW — not when a token expires, not when a CRL propagates
an approval that the action cannot proceed without — not a click the app could skip
RAILS — seven control points, each held by someone other than the runtime, each stopping a specific thing
an act travels the track left to right — and can be stopped at any point by the party that holds that point, without the runtime's cooperation
EVIDENCE — the forensic record the runtime does not own
Every protected step: tool · declared risk · mandate reference · verifier decision · who approved over which digest · tx hash · the digest of the playbook that admitted the run.
Into the owner's vault as a PROV-O graph, a hash-chained audit sink, and a public projection of anchored digests a counterparty can verify without trusting anyone here.
A throttle slows the agent. Rails bound what it can do, let the right person stop it, and leave proof either way.
The kill switch is a revoke transaction: from that block on, every gate refuses and every enforcer reverts — without the runtime's cooperation.
ADR-0057 (admission) · spec 207/221 (custody) · 350 (per-step verification) · 336 §8.3 / 351 (mandates) · 375 (trigger budgets) · 383/395 (receipts, public provenance)
